b:
Hahaha oh man that is some genius writing right there. Let's just forget the fact that the soldier who gets shot and wipes his blood on the protagonist's helmet is white. That's just a failure to pay attention.

What I find funny about this article is the fact that if, as this individual would like to believe, the soldiers are all black then how is that a good thing when you consider the fact that all of the antagonistic forces apart from one mixed-race woman are white. So his idea of this amazing Afrofuturist parable is essentially a world where black people are used as expendable soldiers who are fully controlled by white people with English accents.

Bravo, sir!
Any nation that mandates children to pledge allegiance to a flag in educational settings is misguided.
Hahaha those individuals just love creating nonsense out of nothing, don't they?

You're completely wrong there. Smoking increases the chances of developing lung cancer or heart disease. Nobody has ever said that smoking is the sole cause of lung cancer, and nobody in their right mind has proclaimed that non-smoking-related lung cancer has nothing to do with any other carcinogenic materials they may have ingested.
Pretty sure that's not how he's living his life, friend. What is he supposed to be in constant fear of?

Seriously? Again?

This is yet another example of someone misrepresenting the packaging inserts that come with the vaccines. That is not a list of things CAUSED by the vaccine but a list of things which have been observed post-vaccination. So if someone took the vaccine, got the flu and then reported that to the manufacturer, they'd have to put 'influenza' on that list.

It even says right there that there is nothing to suggest a causal relationship. Some people just aren't very good at reading I suppose.

I, Partridge: We Need to Talk About a Character

It's the fictional autobiography of a much-loved television character from the UK. The book is just incredibly funny and had me in tears on almost every page. It got to the point where I was annoying my housemates with my constant laughter. It is an incredibly funny and well-written book that captures the character's insecurity, vanity, pettiness, and arrogance perfectly.

Needless to say, I had the last laugh...

A wrestler winning the title in a 4-way match with a legendary competitor, a powerhouse, and a former champion on a wrestling show in 1999. He lost the title to the legendary competitor in an exciting match earlier in the night but then got the chance to reclaim it in the main event against the three biggest stars in the promotion.

The wrestler was always my favorite, along with the legendary competitor, and I went absolutely crazy when he won the belt back, and the crowd did too if I remember.

I miss that wrestling promotion...

Well, partly that's the case. Being overweight is seen as a sign of vitality and health. The connection with wealth isn't so pronounced though; especially in smaller communities where people are a lot more familiar with each other.

It seems like you're trying to make a point but I'm not quite seeing what it is...
It's the final sentence I was curious about. Anyway, forget it.
Unfortunately, certain species of birds aren't allowed to practice bird law. Sorry.

You nailed it.

I felt the same about the guardians in the Prequels. After all that wondering what the guardians were really like and being so excited to see them, they turned out to be oblivious jerks.

"You're not training the young one, it's too dangerous."

"But the mentor died and I promised him."

"Ah, okay then, train the boy. What could go wrong?"

They were so inconsistent and so blind to everything that was going on and were just arrogant. The one with the purple lightsaber is the worst culprit. What a tool.

The protagonist is totally right. The guardians thought they were all-knowing and wise and it turned out they were just arrogant and blinded to reality. It makes perfect sense that the protagonist should feel the way they do in the latest installment and that the wise mentor agrees with them.

Couldn't disagree more there, chief!

A character died because they parked on the beach!?! How do you make that stretch? The plan didn't work and was unnecessary. That's the point you're missing. The characters should never have been sent on the mission. The plan was already in place for the evacuation. The mission actually cost more lives because it led to the Rebel plan being given to the opposing force. The character has nothing to do with the other characters and their storyline. Everything the character does is going on without them having any influence over their actions whatsoever. Terrible writing, indeed. People are throwing that line out so much these days and the sad thing is that they do so whilst also displaying a clear lack of understanding of movie writing and plotting.

Why? Do you think that soldiers in war have access to high-level strategy? Was everyone during the major invasion given a full breakdown of the entire operation, or were they just told their parts and given the task of carrying out their own missions?

Exactly.

The officer in charge was respected by the vast majority of the crew because they followed the chain of command. It's only a few individuals who mutiny. Everyone else is getting to the transports without issue. The one causing the problem is not the officer, but rather the dissenting individual.

The captain got demoted. The pilot doesn't recognize the new commander, if you remember. He's heard of her, but he's surprised when he sees that this famous military leader is a slim woman with purple hair. He's all 'THAT'S the admiral!?!'.

The commander says she knows who the pilot is. That's why she knows that he was demoted by the leader. She just knows that the future of the Rebellion should lie in the hands of level-headed strategists who look at the big picture, not arrogant pilots who look at everything through their crosshairs and do things such as losing an entire fleet of bombers on a mission.

Hahaha, there's 'poorly written' again. Despite the fact that her character was very solid, consistent, well-acted, and well-written. She's from a planet that was exploited and persecuted by an oppressive regime, so she and her sister joined the rebellion. Her sister made the ultimate sacrifice, and she has to deal with that in the context of the larger fight.  

That's not a poorly written piece of exposition, and it's not shallow either.

Well, he was in the military organization from when he was essentially a baby. With the organization having a mobile base/command center with a crew of 2.5 million, then it wouldn't be a stretch to imagine that he trained on that flagship at some point. He's had a good 25-odd years on those ships and bases so it doesn't surprise me that he'd know the layouts.

She didn't though. What would the net benefit of him killing himself have been? Would it have destroyed the big weapon or would his rickety little vehicle have disintegrated first? The hero had already made his decision, so they wouldn't have stopped that whole situation. She messed up his chance to selflessly sacrifice himself, sure.
Yep. People just missing details that are right in front of them and blaming their lack of understanding as 'poor communication'.
No he wasn't!!!!! Clearly! He was on the inside and was fed nothing but propaganda from birth! He had no clue how the universe worked.
Exactly. And they try to cover their personal distaste with accusations of 'lazy writing' etc. When in reality, the fault lies with their own inability to understand what's going on in a film.

Why didn’t the resistance ships have time to refuel before evacuating?

Well, how much fuel did they have on the base?

Why didn’t they evacuate earlier?

It seems they went as quickly as possible.

Why are they even evacuating considering the opposing force has been completely devastated at the end of the previous installment?

They haven't been. Look at the leader at the end of the previous film. They're not all 'We're screwed! We're completely devastated by this attack!' Instead, they just instruct their subordinate to bring the key figure back for more training.

So, it's rushed, but also goes on too long? But then it could have been made better by trying to squeeze EVEN MORE into the segment by inserting a character trying to chase them down?

So what is it? Was it rushed? Was it too long? Or did it need more story squeezing in there (somehow making it neither longer, nor more rushed)?

Hmmm...

The authoritarian regime didn't have the character anywhere. He was just there because that's where he was. He's a chancer and a wheeler-dealer. A casino seems like the right place for him. He wasn't a rebel agent. Watch the film again.
Absolutely. I was exactly the same.

Hahahaha, oh right, so because we didn't see wealthy arms dealers from 30 years in the future on a mining platform or on a peaceful planet with little-to-no military presence, it's incongruous? Gimme a break. There's a whole galaxy out there.

..... She is no rebel. 

Er......

That's not a very good comparison. The Republic is a galactic government, not a national one. Their leadership is completely decimated as well as a big chunk of their fleet (we see this in the latest installment) which is in orbit around the capital of the Republic. The New Republic has been crippled. Those who are left evidently ignore the call for help from the Resistance and have abandoned 'the cause'. The Resistance is now the new Rebellion and must do things for themselves.

She was wealthy. She wasn't bad.

It's not 'wealthy = bad' it's 'people who get wealthy selling weapons to a tyrannical regime = bad'.

Absolutely.  

"Duh.... that famous artist is rubbish! That doesn't even look like a real person. Lazy painting!"

No. He attacked the dark side figure because he was trying to protect the young woman. She is his motivation, not the greater good or the ideals of the resistance movement. He wasn't a coward for escaping the oppressive regime. He was brave. Then he confronted them in a significant location. He's not running away out of cowardice; he's running away out of selfishness. That's what changes in the sequel.
It seems you overlooked the main idea.
Good job it doesn't last for an hour, then.
How can this be achieved?

He realizes why he personally needs to get away from the oppressive regime. However, it's over the course of the story that he decides that fighting for the downtrodden is more important than escaping the tyrannical authority. It's not about him realizing the regime is bad, it's about him resolving to fight against it.
Which methods?

Caring about animals being mistreated isn't just an animal rights organization. It fits the attitude of the Rebellion/Resistance perfectly.

One of the most famous quotes from a prominent leader was: “The greatness of a nation and its moral progress can be judged by the way its animals are treated.” 

The story from the distant planet echoes that very well.

It'd be easier if so many people criticizing the film hadn't just completely missed what was right in front of their eyes. They were probably so busy trying to figure out how a certain character could be another that it passed them by.
No, that was the point of the scene.

Well, the problem I have is that people are missing key details and chalking it down to bad writing. When the reality is that they just didn't see it. I think the vocal majority is here now because - as has been discussed at length - they spent 2 years speculating about the previous installment only to have all their theories shot down or ignored.

The previous installment was great fan service. The subsequent installment was something different and that has rankled with people.
Ah, we agree then. My apologies!

So the character was wrong when he said the weapon was charged and the other character's sacrifice would be pointless?

Yes, the mentor sacrifices himself after the other character is rescued, but he was already going to do what he did. He didn't die because of the other character. The other character thought he was going to make a difference. He wasn't. He was blinded by his desire to defeat the oppressive regime and didn't think about the bigger picture. By the end of the film, he reaches the understanding that the mentor had at the start of the movie: "Any victory, no matter how small, is worth fighting for." But the mentor has learned his lesson and tells the other character not to sacrifice himself needlessly. It fits together very nicely.

You've missed a huge chunk of what's going on. The character's mission fails because that's the point. That's the story. He needs to learn his lesson. He sends his companions off on a pointless mission. His rashness puts everyone in danger and he has to learn that lesson.

Again, it's not laziness. It's just people missing key themes.

As I saw the film, the character probably was the codebreaker they were supposed to meet. The fancy guy at the table with the slick hair, moustache, and beautiful women in tow didn't seem to be the kind of person to be having a relationship with the wise character (as she implies). I could see the codebreaker losing his brooch whilst gambling and getting himself thrown in jail more than I could see that other guy being the master codebreaker.

She said he would be wearing the brooch, yes. You don't think someone like that guy would bet that at the casino before getting himself thrown in jail? A friend said she trusted him. She evidently has a history with him. The suave guy in the casino didn't look like that person, to me.

This illegal parking thing is hilarious. You've really focused on the wrong thing here, haha. You could go back through any film - including the original trilogy - and find a dozen characters who the whole story relies on.

"GOD!!! In that space saga, we're expected to believe that the scavengers make their money by salvaging, fixing up and selling droids. But then we're supposed to just accept that they'd try and sell a droid with a bad motivator? Like they'd somehow miss such a common detail like that? LAZY WRITING. A character should never have bought that droid! It's just poor."

"Why does the dark lord spare the Wookiee in that sequel? He doesn't need him. LAZY WRITING!"

"How does the regime build a whole base on that forest moon without the locals fighting back, but then some strangers come and all of a sudden they want to fight? LAZY WRITING!"

I think you're just looking in the wrong places, here.
Yes, that's the theme which the director was trying to get across. He just did it extremely poorly.
Well, you can keep seeing the parking issue as being the crux of the whole film if you like. You'll be pretty much on your own, but that's your prerogative.

Like a certain character, then? 

He has no training beyond a brief lesson on a spaceship, yet he can summon the weapon to his hand in a snowy environment? MARY SUE!
If the film had nothing to do with a popular space opera franchise, it wouldn't be a great movie either.
No, it's the opposite! The dedicated fans have been the most vocal critics because the movie wasn't what they expected.

A character informs another that the weapon is charged and there is no point in proceeding alone. The second character's ship is also disintegrating as he flies towards the weapon. He is not going to succeed; he is heading towards a pointless demise.

> Snoke being able to connect a character and another despite never having met or being close by

How is that a plot hole? It’s not. It’s just a question you have. Are there any rules for force-connections being broken here? Nope. No in-universe rules are broken. There is no plot hole whatsoever. The antagonist hasn't met the character but can sense her. He affected another character from a distance, so we already have precedence for this kind of thing.

> hyperspace ramming being a thing

Again, not a plot hole at all. If it was something people had known about for years, it still wouldn't be a valid tactic for a small group of freedom fighters operating on a limited budget and with limited resources. If they had a significant resource, then fine. But as it is, they just don't have the resources to take their capital ships and use them as weapons. It's not a plot hole at all. Read up on what plot holes are.

> a character never telling another character the plan

She doesn't have to and has reasoning not to. It's the other character who doesn't get this and acts irresponsibly. Not her.

> a character having to stay behind and "steer" despite the ship traveling in a straight line in space and the universe having advanced autopilots

Which autopilots are these? The movie showed pilots staying behind to command ships that were being sacrificed. I can't remember seeing anything in the films which contradicts this.

> why don't the transport ships jump to hyperspace like the escape pod did instead of going to the planet?

Which escape pod? Were those transports equipped with hyperdrives? It seems not.

> the antagonists calling off the attack for no reason

The reason was CLEARLY stated in the film. Watch it again and don't call it a plot hole when it's just you not paying attention.

> the antagonists calling off the attack for no reason

They didn't think they needed to. The commander was happy pursuing them and letting them die slowly.

> a character surviving in space

She uses the Force. You might as well just say that the Force is a plot hole.

> unresolved issues from the last movie like a character's parents

It was resolved. Did you miss that bit of the movie? They were nobodies. They sold her for drinking money or whatever. Resolved. The character has to stop looking to others to give her meaning and has to find it in herself. That was a major plot point. You missed it, obviously.

> a droid activating

He was waiting for a specific character. Seriously. Did you actually watch the previous film and listen to what people said?

> the antagonist's backstory

Not a plot hole at all. Just something you wanted to learn about but didn't. Not knowing who the Emperor was in a previous film wasn't a plot hole.

> a character's students

??? Some sided with the antagonist, the others died. Where's the plot hole?

> a character's map left despite the new movie stating he was going off to die

The map wasn't left by that character. The map was to the first Jedi Temple. Another character figured it out. The map wasn't 'to him', it was to his most likely location.
Well that's our opinion based on this film. You accept the coincidence in other movies but not in this one. Maybe ask yourself why that is.

Why don't we just take a look at the scores then.

The latest installment has a 4.6 on a popular review aggregator, 7.6 on a well-known movie database, and 51% on another review site.

It's lower than all the previous trilogies on the review site and the aggregator, and it has the same score as the third film in the previous trilogy on the movie database.

So yeah, we don't even have to wait to see how many people actually think the previous trilogies are better than this latest installment.

Forget the review site. My family member doesn't go on there to post their scores. This is an internet thing. Don't get so caught up in everything being measured online that you forget the fact that everyday people watch this film and think it's great. There are already plenty of articles highlighting how audience scores have been influenced by online campaigns.

You're doing just that right now. You're saying that there is a "certain feel" to this franchise. That's false. It can be anything.

Well, I agree and disagree. It's all subjective. The previous trilogies didn't feel like the franchise to me. The locations didn't feel right, the characters, the ships, etc. didn't seem right. The displays in the ships were all way in advance of what we saw in the original trilogy, and that didn't make sense to me, for example. To me, the latest installment feels more like the franchise than the second film in the previous trilogy.

The antagonist is still human. He's allowed to have feelings.

Well, I guess that's what's rankling. He has feelings, but not to that same extent. He killed the main villain to save his son, but 'NOOOOOOOOOOO!' just felt so out of place!

I know. And people who hate the latest installment for not going the way they thought are just as petty.

We agree. I just see people who didn't like the latest installment for not being the film they wanted, trying to level all these weak criticisms at it to say it's an objectively bad film and not just one they didn't want.

And he only tells him after the protagonist has already been told so by the antagonist. Had the protagonist never confronted the wise mentor about it, he would have never told him.

True. He keeps his cards close to his chest. Hell, in the latest installment, he knows the new character has taken the ancient texts but he doesn't tell the protagonist. In fact, he allows the protagonist to still believe the texts are in the tree even as it's burning.

Yeah, I guess no one is around to train or be trained. But that doesn't change the fact that there are still a bunch of kids being born with the Force. Just look at those two characters. They weren't part of the order during the original trilogy, but they still believed and could use the Force.

Indeed, but those two are around 35 years before the sequels. They live in a world where there are still temples around. By the time of the latest film, that has all but vanished.

I literally said I understood that in my previous comment.

In the first film, he's trying to escape danger. In the second film, he's trying to escape danger to assist his friend. It's repetitive.

Well, you mentioned that he was starting to align with the Resistance, but that's not what's happening. If I've misunderstood, then fair enough. In the second film, he isn't just running to help his friend. That's his initial motivation, but it changes as the film progresses.

I don't know what you think I was trying to convey. I think it's a poor character arc to have him follow an attractive woman around like a lost puppy for an entire film twice in a row. Clearly, in both films, there's some sort of romantic connection.

It seems pretty clear to me that he is with her because of her skills, not because of any romantic interest. He even pulls back a bit when she kisses him. He's not romantically interested, so how attractive you find her is irrelevant.

I agree that in the bigger picture, the character's actions in destroying the dreadnought were beneficial, but in that moment, he was acting out of bravado and overconfidence. He made the wrong decision at the time, which ultimately turned out to be the right decision overall. The group did not know about hyperspace tracking, so it was a rash choice in that context.

Just because you missed something, doesn't mean you're lacking in intelligence. You might want to reconsider labeling a creator as ineffective at their craft simply because you didn't fully grasp their work.
Yeah. It's pretty simple. There were lots of people who missed the character having the Jedi texts on the ship. People miss things,

“Fuel” has never been an issue in this franchise. The iconic ship was able to fly around for weeks or months without refueling on its way to a notable location.

I’m not sure how long it was between their time on one planet and the next. But I’d assume that the ship was fully fueled at the first location and then refueled at the second. So I'm not sure where the issue is. Where were the other ships last refueled and what did they do before they went to the next destination? We can't answer that so it's not really a contentious point.

After destroying a significant base, everyone at the resistance base was in a relaxed mood, with a character sharing a moment with another, receiving farewells from those around. If they are so worried about a retaliation, then they should already be evacuating.

They took a moment, yes. And then they started evacuating, as we see in the subsequent film.

The previous installment doesn’t give the audience a sense of scale of the opposing force. It looks like they’ve been dealt a massive blow — their base was destroyed, with most of the troops that were stationed there all dead. If the same had happened to the resistance base, then we’d assume they’d be totally wiped out. Obviously, the director really didn’t know himself exactly how big the opposing force’s military power would be, because he knew another director would carve it out and make the decision.

Possibly, although it's never stated that the destroyed base is the home of the opposing force, and the absence of a key figure would imply that it's not and that it's another weapon like a previous infamous one.

I’m sure we’ll find out later that the opposing fleet will dwarf the size of the previous regime’s fleet, because of course it does.

I'm sure it does now that the significant base wiped out much of the fleet.

How so? As of the latest installment, the Republic has been decimated by a powerful weapon. They didn't listen to the likes of a prominent leader and they paid the price. The Resistance now has very few - if any - allies.
I'm not sure what you mean as I thought the character's development was pretty clear.

You're completely misrepresenting the film. Putting things out of order. Skipping chunks. Whatever. If you think that a character saying 'Rebel scum' had no clear build-up, then I'm afraid I can't help you.

It's so tiring, all this. People used to just say, 'I didn't like that line,' and now they feel the need to show how that line demonstrates fundamental flaws in the entire movie when nothing could be farther from the truth.

I hope you enjoy the next films more.

Read the books if you want more. The specific series in particular explains the new government and military setup.  

The information you want is out there.

It's not quite the same thing. The character isn't abandoning the Rebellion by going to save his friends; he's cutting short his training.  

I didn't say the character was selfish, just that he has his own motivations which initially aren't related to the conflict between the Resistance and the First Order.

Think about what happened and what was said in that film. The guardians are finished. The guardians' order died with the last master. His lesson to the new apprentice was to treat the energy differently. Yes, a new kind of guardian will emerge now, but the last master really was the final guardian and the old ways died with him.

Yes, the new apprentice has the texts, but they are the original/ancient writings and that's not the same as the bloated and arrogant guardians' order which grew up over millennia. 

Edit: didn't make much sense.
No, they'd say, 'fair enough, you don't have to'.
Or just say you don't like it and not go on a pretentious rant about poor writing.

Nah, I made a point about the fact that there are lots of people who are throwing out things like, "It's just lazy writing" when it simply appears they've missed things in the film which were obvious to others. People saying various things are plot holes ("Why did the character just die?") when they've just missed important bits of information in the film.

There's no strawman either, I'm just making fun.

Yeah, I didn't mind it one bit. They were really pushed for time. They had to get in and out as quickly as possible, so they landed their vessel anywhere they could and made their way to the entertainment venue as quickly as possible.

But yeah, we all have different things that can take us out of a film.

Yeah, it's the same with that character. I'm so bored of their TERRIBLE character who doesn't go anywhere.

Film IV: The character goes on a mission to rescue somebody.

Film V: The character goes on a mission to rescue somebody (again!), along with others.

Film VI: The character goes on a mission to rescue somebody.

and now....

Film VIII: The character finished their life by going on a mission to rescue somebody.

They're probably the worst character ever written. Such lazy writing.

Ah, right. I thought you might be. I enjoyed the back story, but the stuff I actually enjoyed most about it came in the expanded universe. The stuff in the films was pretty boring and confusing. Like, who the heck was that character? It got explained in the books, but that part was just plain confusing.

Anyway, as for plot holes... Oh man! There are really too many to list and they begin right at the start of the first film! The antagonists' plan is to kill the Jedi, right? But they wait for the Jedi to leave their ship and sit in a conference room. Then they try to poison the Jedi and they blow up the ship they arrive in. Erm... Guys? You could have fixed this whole thing by just blowing up the ship as it landed in your hangar bay. D'oh!

And then it goes from there... Ad nauseum right up to one Jedi forgetting he can use his abilities (like at the start of the movie) right when he needs it most if he's going to reach his companion and the other character before the energy shields close in the power station.

Haha, we didn't have that in the UK. However, I 'watched' a wrestling event from '99 via a 'live stream' which was a semi-regular text commentary along with a live, blurry image that refreshed every minute. 

At the time I thought I had entered the future. I was watching a wrestling pay-per-view LIVE! Normally we had to wait for the VHS to come out (if ever) so this was seriously cool. The only strong image which sticks in my mind is a wrestler fighting with another during the ladder match.... *sigh*

Great times...
So.... kinda like a powerful regime then?
Ugh, that terrible theme.

I really enjoyed the recent wrestling match! I don't watch every week, but I loved the change in style that came with that event. I appreciated how one wrestler choked out the other and was just grappling with him for most of the match. It wasn't a classic battle, but I really enjoyed the character of the wrestler.

So a certain pilot character is also a bit redundant or just a poorly developed character? He survived two major space station attacks where he was involved right up to the end and a significant battle. We don't get a big backstory to explain everything about why he's a great pilot. We just accept that he is a great pilot.

These kinds of reactions seem to show me that we've been spoiled rotten. We've had so much content from this franchise with all this backstory and detail that people are now annoyed they're not getting that detail in the films when in reality, we never got those details in the first place. Sure, the earlier films shoved a lot of exposition in there, and they were poorly received. I'd rather have a good movie that trusts its audience to be intelligent and capable of following and being invested in a film without having the plot and backstory explained to them at every step along the way. That's what certain popular thrillers are for.
Well all three of the TIE fighters that the dark side user attacked were destroyed, so evidently there is a threat.

Nope. The earlier films took 3 installments to explain where the authoritarian regime and the dark figure came from. They were prequels, which means we already know where everything ends up once they're finished. They are explaining how things got to a point that we already know about.

The later films are set 30 years AFTER the previous installment. We know nothing about that time period, just as we knew nothing when the original trilogy was released. It is absolutely NOT the job of the sequel films to explain what happened in the 30 years prior to them starting! No reason at all and certainly no more reason to explain everything than the first film had. These films are moving forward into unknown territory, not simply giving us backstory like the prequels (which were not well-received!) so getting bogged down in explaining the past simply isn't an option. Read the books if that's what you're after.

We know that both the Jedi of the Republic and the forces of the Empire were actively searching for individuals sensitive to the Force, so it doesn't really make sense that a character like Snoke just appears from nowhere... let alone appears from nowhere to build a new order and create numerous superweapons within decades of the Empire's fall. It prevents you from suspending disbelief because it's not really internally consistent anymore.

Well, we know that this character was based in a mysterious and largely unexplored region. That is the UNKNOWN region, which suggests some kind of mystery or unknown quality to the area. Almost as if it would be a great place to remain hidden. We also know that a powerful dark side figure felt a strong presence in this region and sent people out to investigate.

So the fact that the Jedi didn't find this character when he was living outside of Republic space makes sense. But why do you say he 'appears from nowhere'? Who says he did that? Again, this is 30 years after the previous major conflict. He no more 'appears from nowhere' than any other character in the films. You're filling in the blanks yourself and using your own interpretations as arguments against the film. It's already been stated that the new order attracted many remnants of the Empire, and the fact that they've had 30 years to expand their forces through conquest of the unknown region doesn't seem very far-fetched to me at all.

As for the character's influence over another character, we learned in the first film of the new trilogy that he turned to the dark side while training with a prominent Jedi. That makes sense by itself. But with the second film, we learn that it was actually this mysterious figure who turned him to the dark side. That doesn't really make sense -- how was he tempted by this figure if he was training with the Jedi?

That was actually revealed in the first film of the new trilogy. This character has been influencing the other character pretty much since before he was born (more details in a related novel, if I remember correctly). By the time the Jedi realized how corrupted he had become, it was too late.

Well, a character does the same thing to another character and tries to do it to a third character. A well-known villain reads a young hero's mind in a popular film, and another antagonist speaks to the hero as though he can read his thoughts.
What hype around the character? The excitement came from the fans, not the creators of the film.

It could go an infinite number of places really, and they'd all be new.

Yeah, but would they be good?

I don't think a certain character should have been the motive for another character's turn to the dark side.

I'm not sure they were. A powerful figure had been influencing the character since before birth, and when another character read their mind, they saw that they were already lost to the dark side. However, the moment provided by the first character definitely allowed the second character to become who they are.
